issues.legal_issue: A final determination between the parties that a religious group is entitled to administer a temple cannot be reopened in later litigation between them merely by relying on subsequent interpretations of law or disputing the group’s qualification to administer the temple.
material_facts: An earlier judgment between the temple administrators and the State had recognized the administrators as a religious denomination or section and recognized their right to participate in administering the temple.
The State’s appeal from that judgment was dismissed after the State withdrew the notification that had prompted the dispute, and the determination became final.

In the later proceedings, the administrators again challenged State action affecting their administration of the temple, and the High Court reconsidered whether the earlier determination bound the parties.
issues.conclusion: The earlier determination was binding between the parties, and the High Court could not sit in appeal over it or re-examine the administrators’ status and right to administer the temple. State authorities could not deny those previously determined rights through later orders.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of res judicata applies to writ proceedings and makes a final determination between the same parties conclusive in later litigation, even if the earlier decision is alleged to be erroneous or a later interpretation of law might differ. A final judgment must be given effect unless reversed or modified by an appellate authority. Article 26 protects the rights of religious denominations, and Section 107 of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959 preserves those rights. The Court relied on Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Deorajin Debi, Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd. v. Janapada Sabha Chhindwara, Hope Plantations Ltd. v. Taluk Land Board, Union of India v. Nanak Singh, and other authorities on finality and res judicata.

predicates.later_proceeding_between_same_parties: A later court proceeding takes place between the same parties, or their relevant successors, as an earlier proceeding.
predicates.prior_final_judgment_decided_same_issue: An earlier final judgment between those parties decided the issue raised again in the later proceeding.

issues.definition: When the same parties bring a later proceeding over an issue already decided by an earlier final judgment, the earlier determination controls the later proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: An executive officer cannot be appointed under a statutory power made subject to prescribed conditions when no rules prescribe the conditions governing that appointment.
material_facts: A statutory authority appointed an executive officer to manage the temple and assigned the officer duties concerning the temple’s administration and property.
The governing statute made appointment subject to conditions to be prescribed, but no rules prescribing the conditions for such appointments had been framed.
The appointment order did not state the reasons or circumstances that made the appointment necessary.
issues.conclusion: The executive officer could not lawfully have been appointed in the absence of rules prescribing the conditions for appointment, and the appointment order was invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 45 of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959 makes appointment of an executive officer subject to conditions prescribed by rules. Section 116 authorizes rules to be made for the purposes of the Act. “Prescribed” means prescribed by rules, and a statutory power conditioned on prescription cannot be exercised without the required rules. The Court relied on Manohar Lal Chopra v. Rai Bahadur Rao Raja Seth Hiralal, Hindustan Ideal Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation v. Babu Goverdhan Regular Motor Service, and Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd. v. BPL Mobile Cellular Ltd.

predicates.executive_officer_appointment_case: The proceeding concerns an appointment of an executive officer to manage a religious institution.
predicates.appointment_subject_to_prescribed_condit: The governing law makes the appointment subject to conditions that must be prescribed.
predicates.no_rules_prescribe_appointment_condition: No rules prescribe the conditions governing the appointment.

issues.definition: When an executive officer appointment is subject to prescribed conditions but no rules prescribe those conditions, the appointment is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A State takeover of a religious denomination’s administration to remedy mismanagement must be temporary and cannot continue indefinitely after the remedial purpose has been served.
material_facts: The administrators had a previously recognized right to administer the temple and its properties.
The executive officer’s order placed temple property, income, offerings, and staff under the officer’s control.
The order did not prescribe a period for which the officer’s appointment or takeover would remain in force.
The order did not disclose the reasons or circumstances necessitating the appointment.
issues.conclusion: A takeover of administration must be limited to a period reasonably connected to remedying the mismanagement; the order was unsustainable because it prescribed no duration. The statutory power to regulate could not be used to supersede the administrators indefinitely.
issues.legal_principle: Article 26(d) protects a religious denomination’s right to administer its property in accordance with law, and Section 107 of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959 preserves Article 26 rights. State regulation may address mismanagement, but supersession must be temporary and end when the mismanagement is remedied; regulation does not authorize permanent replacement of the administration. The Court relied on Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Tirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, Sri Sri Sri Lakshamana Yatendrulu v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Ratilal Panachand Gandhi v. State of Bombay, Pannalal Bansilal Pitti v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and K. Ramanathan v. State of Tamil Nadu.

predicates.religious_institution_management_takeove: The proceeding concerns State or statutory-authority control over the administration of a religious institution.
predicates.takeover_intended_to_remedy_mismanagemen: The control is imposed to address alleged mismanagement or maladministration.
predicates.no_fixed_duration: The takeover order specifies no duration or endpoint tied to remedying the identified problem.

issues.definition: When State control over a religious institution is imposed to remedy mismanagement but has no fixed duration tied to that purpose, the indefinite takeover is invalid.
